title: aircrack-ng
description: A complete suite of tools for auditing Wi-Fi network security: monitoring, attacking, testing, and cracking 802.11 wireless protocols. For legal use only — auditing networks and hardware you own or are explicitly authorized to test.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
## What is aircrack-ng?

`aircrack-ng` is not a single program — it's a **suite** of command-line tools built around one goal: assessing the security of Wi-Fi (802.11) networks. It covers four broad areas:

- **Monitoring** — capturing raw 802.11 frames off the air (`airodump-ng`).
- **Attacking** — replaying traffic, deauthenticating clients, creating fake access points to test how a network responds (`aireplay-ng`, `airbase-ng`).
- **Testing** — checking Wi-Fi card and driver capabilities for injection support (`aireplay-ng --test`).
- **Cracking** — recovering keys once enough data has been captured, for WEP and WPA/WPA2-PSK (`aircrack-ng`, `aircrack-ng` + GPU tools like `hashcat`).

All tools are scriptable and command-line driven, which makes the suite easy to automate and to script into larger audit workflows.

> **Legal and ethical use only.** These tools let you deauthenticate clients, capture credentials-adjacent handshake data, and brute-force keys. Running them against a network you do not own, and do not have **explicit written permission** to test, is illegal in most countries (in the US, it can fall under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; most other countries have equivalent computer-misuse laws). Every example in this documentation uses a Wi-Fi access point the reader owns and controls.

## 1. Install

On Arch Linux:

```bash
sudo pacman -S aircrack-ng
```

On Debian/Ubuntu:

```bash
sudo apt install aircrack-ng
```

From source (all platforms, if you want the bleeding-edge version):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aircrack-ng/aircrack-ng.git
cd aircrack-ng
autoreconf -i
./configure --with-experimental
make
sudo make install
```

## 2. Hardware requirement: monitor mode + injection

The single biggest blocker for beginners isn't the software — it's the **Wi-Fi adapter**. Most laptop-internal Wi-Fi chips do not support:

- **Monitor mode** — capturing all frames on a channel, not just ones addressed to you.
- **Packet injection** — sending crafted 802.11 frames (needed for deauth and replay attacks).

Check your card:

```bash
airmon-ng
```

This lists wireless interfaces and the chipset driver behind each one. Popular chipsets known to support both monitor mode and injection include Atheros (`ath9k_htc`), Ralink (`rt2800usb`), and the well-known **Alfa AWUS036ACH / AWUS036NHA** USB adapters, which is why most people learning this suite buy a dedicated USB Wi-Fi adapter rather than relying on a laptop's built-in card.

## 3. Core concepts

- **Monitor mode vs managed mode** — managed mode is the normal state your Wi-Fi card runs in (associated to one AP). Monitor mode puts the radio into a passive listening state across all traffic on a channel, which is required before capturing.
- **BSSID** — the MAC address of the access point's radio.
- **Handshake (WPA/WPA2)** — a 4-way EAPOL exchange between a client and an AP during association, which encodes the pieces needed to verify a candidate password offline. Capturing this handshake is the goal of most WPA/WPA2 auditing.
- **IV (Initialization Vector)** — relevant to the older, broken WEP protocol; WEP cracking works by collecting enough IVs to statistically recover the key, which is why WEP is considered cryptographically broken today.
- **PMKID** — a newer, faster capture technique (no client needed) supported by `hcxdumptool`/`hcxtools` and usable with `aircrack-ng`/`hashcat`, useful when no client ever connects during your capture window.

## 4. The basic workflow

Every WPA/WPA2 audit with this suite follows the same four steps:

1. Put your card into monitor mode (`airmon-ng`).
2. Discover networks and pick a target BSSID + channel (`airodump-ng`).
3. Capture a handshake, optionally speeding this up with a deauth (`airodump-ng` + `aireplay-ng`).
4. Crack the captured handshake against a wordlist (`aircrack-ng`).

The **Learn by Example** section walks through this entire loop end-to-end against a router you own, with real commands and real output to expect at each step.

Guides.Tool Overview:
## The core tools

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `airmon-ng` | Enable/disable monitor mode on a wireless interface; lists interfaces and detects conflicting processes. |
| `airodump-ng` | Packet capture: lists nearby networks/clients, and writes `.cap` files used by every other tool. |
| `aireplay-ng` | Frame injection: deauth attacks, ARP replay, fake authentication, fragmentation attacks. |
| `aircrack-ng` | The actual key-recovery engine: WEP statistical attacks and WPA/WPA2 dictionary/PMK attacks against captured data. |
| `airbase-ng` | Turns your card into a fake access point, useful for client-side testing and honeypot-style AP auditing. |
| `airdecap-ng` | Decrypts WEP/WPA capture files once you have the key, for further analysis in Wireshark. |
| `airolib-ng` | Precomputes and stores PMKs for a set of ESSIDs, dramatically speeding up repeated dictionary attacks. |
| `packetforge-ng` | Crafts custom encrypted packets for injection, used in advanced WEP attacks. |

## Putting a card into monitor mode

```bash
sudo airmon-ng check kill   # stop NetworkManager/wpa_supplicant so they don't interfere
sudo airmon-ng start wlan0  # renames interface to something like wlan0mon
```

`airmon-ng check kill` matters because `NetworkManager` and `wpa_supplicant` constantly try to re-manage the interface, which will silently knock it out of monitor mode mid-capture — a very common beginner gotcha.

## Scanning for networks

```bash
sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon
```

This prints a live-updating table of BSSIDs, channel, signal power, encryption (WEP/WPA/WPA2/WPA3), and ESSID (network name), plus a second table of associated client MAC addresses underneath. Note the **channel** and **BSSID** of your target — you'll need both for a focused capture.

## Focused capture on one network

```bash
sudo airodump-ng --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF --channel 6 --write capture wlan0mon
```

- `--bssid` locks the capture to one access point, filtering out neighboring network noise.
- `--channel` avoids the default channel-hopping behavior, which matters because a handshake frame is only reliably captured if you're parked on the right channel when it happens.
- `--write capture` writes `capture-01.cap` (and companion files) to disk — this `.cap` file is the artifact every later step operates on.

Watch the top-right corner of the `airodump-ng` UI: once a handshake is captured it prints `WPA handshake: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF`.

## Speeding up capture with a deauth

Handshakes only happen when a client associates. Rather than waiting, you can force a reconnect on a client that's already connected — since it's your own device, forcing it to reconnect is harmless:

```bash
sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 11:22:33:44:55:66 wlan0mon
```

- `--deauth 5` sends 5 deauthentication frames.
- `-a` is the AP's BSSID, `-c` is the target client's MAC.
- The client will automatically reconnect within a second or two, generating a fresh 4-way handshake for `airodump-ng` to capture in the background.

## Cracking a captured handshake

```bash
aircrack-ng -w /path/to/wordlist.txt -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF capture-01.cap
```

`aircrack-ng` derives a PMK from each candidate password in the wordlist and compares it against the captured handshake material. This is why **wordlist quality matters more than raw CPU speed** for beginners — a well-known starting wordlist is `rockyou.txt`, included in many security-focused Linux distributions or downloadable for local, personal testing.

## Speeding up repeated attacks: airolib-ng

If you're auditing several APs that might share password patterns (e.g. a chain of routers you manage), pre-computing PMKs per ESSID avoids redoing the expensive key-derivation step every time:

```bash
airolib-ng pmk.db --import essid essid-list.txt
airolib-ng pmk.db --import passwd wordlist.txt
airolib-ng pmk.db --batch
aircrack-ng -r pmk.db capture-01.cap
```

## WEP: why it's included but rarely needed today

WEP is cryptographically broken and essentially extinct on real networks, but the WEP attack chain is still commonly taught because it demonstrates classic IV-collection statistical attacks:

```bash
sudo aireplay-ng --arpreplay -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -h 11:22:33:44:55:66 wlan0mon
aircrack-ng capture-01.cap
```

If you want hands-on WEP practice, set an old router (that you own) to WEP mode specifically for the exercise — no currently-shipping consumer router defaults to WEP, so this is a deliberate lab-only setup.

## PMKID: capture without a connected client

```bash
hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=1
hcxpcapngtool capture.pcapng -o hashes.22000
aircrack-ng hashes.22000 -w wordlist.txt
```

Useful when no client is currently associated (so a deauth-triggered handshake isn't available) — most modern consumer routers still respond to a PMKID request during initial association attempts.

Learn by Example.Overview:
## Learning aircrack-ng through real projects

The fastest way to actually understand this suite is to build a small **home lab**: one router you own, one Wi-Fi adapter that supports monitor mode + injection, and one old phone or laptop to act as a "victim" client. Every project below uses only hardware and networks you control.

| # | Project | What it teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Build a Home Wi-Fi Audit Lab](/aircrack-ng/build-a-home-wi-fi-audit-lab/) | Hardware selection, monitor mode setup, verifying injection support |
| 2 | [Capture and Crack Your Own WPA2 Handshake](/aircrack-ng/capture-and-crack-your-own-wpa2-handshake/) | The full airodump-ng → aireplay-ng → aircrack-ng workflow |
| 3 | [Auditing Router Firmware Defaults](/aircrack-ng/auditing-router-firmware-defaults/) | Why default/weak PSKs fail instantly, building a targeted wordlist |
| 4 | [Build a Rogue AP Honeypot with airbase-ng](/aircrack-ng/build-a-rogue-ap-honeypot-with-airbase-ng/) | Client-side attack surface, evil-twin detection, defensive takeaways |
| 5 | [Automating a Recurring Home Network Audit](/aircrack-ng/automating-a-recurring-home-network-audit/) | Scripting the suite with Dart for scheduled self-audits |

Each project below is self-contained, but they build in difficulty — start with Project 1 if you don't already have monitor-mode hardware confirmed working.

> Reminder: every command below targets `AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF` / `MyHomeNetwork` as placeholders for **your own** router's BSSID and ESSID. Never substitute a BSSID you don't have explicit authorization to test.
Learn by Example.Project 1: Build a Home Wi-Fi Audit Lab:
## Goal

Confirm your hardware can do everything the rest of this guide needs, before you touch a real handshake.

## What you need

- A USB Wi-Fi adapter known to support monitor mode + injection (Atheros AR9271-based adapters like the Alfa AWUS036NHA are the classic beginner recommendation — cheap, well-supported by the mainline Linux kernel, no out-of-tree driver compiling required).
- Your own home router, with admin access to its settings page.
- A second device (old phone, spare laptop) to act as a test client.

## Steps

1. **Confirm the adapter is recognized:**

   ```bash
   lsusb
   iw dev
   ```

2. **Put it into monitor mode:**

   ```bash
   sudo airmon-ng check kill
   sudo airmon-ng start wlan1
   iwconfig
   ```

   You should see `Mode:Monitor` on the renamed interface (often `wlan1mon`).

3. **Verify injection actually works** (this is the step people skip, then wonder why capture attacks silently fail):

   ```bash
   sudo aireplay-ng --test wlan1mon
   ```

   A working setup reports something like `Injection is working!` alongside a list of nearby APs it successfully pinged. If this fails, the adapter or driver doesn't support injection — check the aircrack-ng project's compatibility list before buying hardware.

4. **Log your own network's details** for later projects:

   ```bash
   sudo airodump-ng wlan1mon
   ```

   Write down your router's BSSID and channel — you'll reuse these constants throughout the rest of the lab.

## What you learned

The difference between a card that merely *claims* monitor-mode support in software and one that can actually inject frames — the single most common reason beginners get stuck before they've run a single real attack.
Learn by Example.Project 2: Capture and Crack Your Own WP:
## Goal

Run the complete audit loop against your own router end-to-end, and understand every field `aircrack-ng` prints along the way.

## Setup

Make sure your test client (phone/laptop from Project 1) is actively connected to your home Wi-Fi.

## Steps

1. **Start a focused capture, writing to disk:**

   ```bash
   sudo airodump-ng --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF --channel 6 \
     --write homelab-capture wlan1mon
   ```

2. **In a second terminal, force your test client to reconnect:**

   ```bash
   sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF \
     -c 11:22:33:44:55:66 wlan1mon
   ```

   Watch the first terminal — within a few seconds you should see `WPA handshake: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF` appear in the top-right status line.

3. **Stop the capture** (`Ctrl+C`) once the handshake line appears.

4. **Crack it** using a wordlist that includes your actual password somewhere in it (for the exercise, temporarily add your real Wi-Fi password into a test wordlist file so you can confirm success, then switch to a large public wordlist like `rockyou.txt` to see how long a *real* attack takes against your password's strength):

   ```bash
   echo "your-actual-wifi-password" >> test-wordlist.txt
   aircrack-ng -w test-wordlist.txt -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF homelab-capture-01.cap
   ```

5. **Re-run against `rockyou.txt`** (no known-good password included) to see realistic timing:

   ```bash
   aircrack-ng -w rockyou.txt -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF homelab-capture-01.cap
   ```

## What you learned

- How a handshake actually gets on the wire (client reconnection, not magic).
- That `aircrack-ng`'s cracking speed is dictated by wordlist size and password complexity, not the tool itself — this is the practical argument for long, high-entropy Wi-Fi passwords.
- If your real router password survived the `rockyou.txt` run, you've just empirically verified your own network's PSK strength.
Learn by Example.Project 3: Auditing Router Firmware Defa:
## Goal

Many routers ship with predictable default passwords or SSID-derived defaults (e.g. serial-number-based PSKs printed on a sticker). This project teaches you to build a **targeted** wordlist instead of relying purely on generic ones like `rockyou.txt`.

## Steps

1. **Inspect your router's default password scheme.** Flip it over — many consumer routers print a default PSK on a physical label, often derived from the device's serial number or MAC address using a documented (or reverse-engineered) algorithm.

2. **Reset your router to factory defaults** temporarily (only on hardware you own, and only for this exercise) so it's using its original default PSK.

3. **Build a small, targeted wordlist** based on the pattern you observed (e.g. if the default looks like `WIFI-XXXXXXXX` where X is derived from the MAC, generate the plausible candidate space):

   ```bash
   python3 -c "
   mac_suffix = 'DDEEFF'
   for i in range(0, 100):
       print(f'WIFI-{mac_suffix}{i:02d}')
   " > targeted-wordlist.txt
   ```

4. **Capture and crack against your targeted list**, following the same `airodump-ng` → `aireplay-ng` → `aircrack-ng` steps from Project 2, but pointing `-w` at `targeted-wordlist.txt`.

5. **Reconfigure your router with a strong custom PSK** afterward and confirm the same targeted wordlist now fails.

## What you learned

Why security guidance universally says "change the default Wi-Fi password" — a targeted wordlist built from a known default-generation pattern cracks in seconds, regardless of how strong `aircrack-ng`'s underlying cryptographic attack is.
Learn by Example.Project 4: Build a Rogue AP Honeypot wit:
## Goal

Understand the *client-side* half of Wi-Fi security — how easily a device can be tricked into joining a fake access point — by building your own "evil twin" of your home network and observing how your own devices react.

## Steps

1. **Clone your own network's ESSID as a fake open AP:**

   ```bash
   sudo airbase-ng -e "MyHomeNetwork" -c 6 wlan1mon
   ```

   This creates a new interface, typically `at0`, representing the fake AP's wired side.

2. **Bridge or NAT `at0` to give it working internet** (optional, but makes the honeypot convincing enough to observe real client behavior):

   ```bash
   sudo ifconfig at0 up 10.0.0.1 netmask 255.255.255.0
   sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wlan0 -j MASQUERADE
   ```

3. **Walk your test phone near both networks** and watch whether it auto-joins the fake open one instead of your real WPA2 one. Most phones prefer previously-joined networks by SSID name alone, which is exactly the weakness evil-twin attacks exploit in the wild.

4. **Turn it around — defensive takeaway:** check whether your phone's Wi-Fi settings let you disable auto-join for open networks, or require a saved network to also match a specific BSSID rather than just an SSID string.

## What you learned

The client side of Wi-Fi trust is often weaker than the AP side — this is exactly why security-conscious organizations deploy WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation, where a client can cryptographically confirm it's talking to the real AP infrastructure and won't silently join a same-named impostor.

Project.FAQ:
### Is it legal to use aircrack-ng?

The software itself is legal to possess and run everywhere. What's regulated is *what you point it at*. Using it against your own hardware, or a network you have explicit written authorization to test (e.g. as part of a paid penetration-testing engagement with a signed scope document), is legal in essentially every jurisdiction. Using it against any other network — a neighbor's Wi-Fi, a coffee shop's guest network, anything you don't own or have permission for — is a criminal offense in most countries, regardless of intent.

### My built-in laptop Wi-Fi doesn't work with airmon-ng — why?

Most integrated laptop Wi-Fi chipsets (common Intel and Broadcom parts especially) either don't support monitor mode at all, or support monitor mode but not packet injection. This is a hardware/firmware limitation, not something Aircrack-ng or its drivers can patch around — a supported USB adapter is the standard fix.

### `aireplay-ng --deauth` isn't working against my own AP — why?

Common causes: your card doesn't actually support injection (re-run the `--test` check from Project 1), you're deauthing on the wrong channel, or (increasingly common on modern routers) **Protected Management Frames (802.11w)** are enabled, which cryptographically signs deauth/disassociation frames and makes unauthenticated deauth attacks ineffective — this is in fact the modern defense against exactly this attack, and it's part of the WPA3 standard.

### Does aircrack-ng work against WPA3?

Not directly in the same way as WPA2. WPA3-Personal replaces the 4-way-handshake-based PSK exchange with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which is resistant to offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake. Networks running WPA3 in its full, non-transitional mode are not vulnerable to the classic `airodump-ng`/`aircrack-ng` handshake-capture-and-crack workflow described in this guide.

### Where can I practice legally beyond my own home network?

Deliberately vulnerable practice environments exist for exactly this purpose — for example, setting up your own isolated `hostapd`-based access point on a spare Raspberry Pi, which gives you a fully controlled, fully legal target with no ambiguity about authorization.
